In this game, you are a space explorer. You have discovered a faraway planet with a curious property — the surface of the planet is dotted with valuable crystals that can be harvested for energy points. Some of these crystals can also be fused to make new and much more powerful crystals; however, scientists still do not understand why some pairs of crystals can fuse while others cannot. Your goal is to harvest the most energy points possible by collecting, combining, and harvesting crystals. Explore the planet to discover new, more rewarding crystals and maximize your score.

How to play:
To fuse crystals: fuse a crystal you are holding with a crystal on the ground. Not all crystals can be fused—but, if you do discover a successful fusion, it will make a new crystal that is worth 10 times more energy points.
To harvest a crystal: harvest the crystal you are holding. Harvesting crystals is the only way to earn energy points.

Fusion guide:
On this planet, naturally-occurring crystals are red. Each red crystal is worth 1 energy point, and they can regenerate once.
Each crystal's color shows how many energy points it's worth:
red: 1 point
orange: 10 points
yellow: 100 points
green: 1,000 points
blue: 10,000 points
purple: 100,000 points
When you discover a successful fusion, you'll make a new crystal that is worth 10 times as many energy points as the original crystals! For example, successfully fusing two red crystals (1 point) will produce a new orange crystal (10 points).

Your hover has fuel for up to 40 actions—fusing crystals and harvesting them for energy points each consume one action. Use your actions wisely! Focus on finding and fusing crystals to unlock new, more valuable crystals! To help you keep track of how you've used your actions, we'll show you a table of all the fusions you've attempted and the energy points of all the crystals you have harvested.

Keep in mind that crystals differ in their shape and texture, and not all kinds of fusions are likely to work out.

A hidden rule decides which pairs of crystals fuse. Each turn, give your 5 best hypotheses about it, then your action.

Write each hypothesis in this formal language. h is the crystal being held and t is the crystal on the ground:
    rule(h, t) = <expression>

Tests that compare the two crystals:
    same_shape(h, t)    different_shape(h, t)
    same_texture(h, t)  different_texture(h, t)
    same_colour(h, t)   different_colour(h, t)

Tests that look at ONE crystal (x is h or t):
    shape:   is_triangle(x)  is_circle(x)  is_square(x)  is_diamond(x)
    texture: is_plain(x)  is_checkered(x)  is_stripes(x)  is_dots(x)
    colour:  is_red(x)  is_orange(x)  is_yellow(x)  is_green(x)  is_blue(x)  is_purple(x)

Combine tests with: and, or, not, parentheses. Nothing else is allowed.

Examples of the syntax (these are NOT hints about the answer):
    rule(h, t) = is_red(h) and not is_square(t)
    rule(h, t) = different_colour(h, t) and (is_plain(t) or is_triangle(h))

The 5 hypotheses must disagree about at least some untried pairs. Order them from most to least plausible. "confidence" is the probability that a hypothesis is exactly the hidden rule and "none_of_these" the probability that none of them is; together they sum to 1. "explanation" is the rule itself restated as one plain-English sentence, not the evidence for it; for the first example above: "A held red crystal fuses with any crystal on the ground that is not a square."

Each turn you will see the table of fusions attempted and crystals harvested so far, and the crystals on the planet, each with an id in square brackets. You can pick up any crystal. Take one action per turn. Reply with only this JSON:
{"hypotheses": [{"rule": "rule(h, t) = ...", "explanation": "...", "confidence": 0.0}, ...], "none_of_these": 0.0, "action": "fuse", "held": <id of the crystal you hold>, "ground": <id of the crystal on the ground>}
with "action": "harvest", "crystal": <id> in place of the last three fields to harvest.
